lessons.title: The Scramble for Africa and the Berlin Conference

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain the economic, political and social causes of the Scramble
Describe the Berlin Conference (1884–85) and its rules
reviewNotes: Verify: conference dates (15 Nov 1884–26 Feb 1885); Bismarck host; participants; effective occupation; Fashoda 1898; Ethiopia and Liberia in 1914.
Check emphasis of the syllabus on causes.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Causes
blocks.md: **Economic:** raw materials (rubber, palm oil, minerals), new markets and investment. **Political and strategic:** national prestige, rivalry between Britain, France and Germany, control of trade routes. **Social and humanitarian:** missionary movements and the claim to end the slave trade and ‘civilise’ Africa. **Technology:** steamships, quinine against malaria, rifles and the telegraph made inland conquest possible.

blocks.title: The Berlin Conference
blocks.md: Called by Germany’s chancellor Otto von Bismarck, it met in Berlin from **November 1884 to February 1885** with European powers, the United States and the Ottoman Empire present; no African ruler took part. Agreements: free trade and navigation on the Congo and Niger, the recognition of King Leopold II’s Congo claim, and a rule that claims to coastal territory needed **effective occupation** and notification to other powers.

blocks.caption: The Scramble for Africa, 1870–1914.
blocks.alt: Timeline with events 1884 Berlin Conference opens, 1885 Berlin Act, 1898 Fashoda and 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia independent.

blocks.title: Consequences
blocks.md: The conference did not itself divide Africa, but it set rules for competition. By 1914 almost all of Africa was under European control; only **Ethiopia and Liberia** remained independent. Borders drawn in Europe cut across peoples or joined unlike ones. Africans resisted in many places and used diplomacy, but were often defeated by superior weapons.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Berlin Conference did not ‘start’ colonialism or draw the whole map: it set rules; borders were agreed later.
- African rulers were not invited to the conference.
- Effective occupation concerned coastal claims and meant real presence, not just flags.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Rank causes
blocks.statement: Which cause was most important? Argue briefly for economic causes.
steps: Industrial Europe needed raw materials and markets.
Political rivalry was partly rivalry over economic gain, so economics linked to many other causes.
blocks.answer: Economic causes are strong but connected to others.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Effects of arbitrary borders
blocks.statement: Explain one long-term effect of the way Africa’s borders were drawn.
steps: Borders ignored language, culture and trade routes.
Peoples were split among several countries, while unlike groups were joined.
This created challenges for national unity and cross-border cooperation after independence.

objectives: Describe the establishment of German rule
reviewNotes: Verify: treaty July 1884; Neukamerun 1911; Rudolf Duala Manga Bell executed August 1914; main crops; railway names and dates (not given here).

blocks.title: Establishment
blocks.md: In July 1884 Germany made treaties with Duala chiefs and declared a protectorate, **Kamerun** (1884). Over the next years German officials, soldiers and companies pushed inland, signing treaties and fighting those who resisted. In **1911**, after an agreement with France, Kamerun was enlarged by territory to the south and east (**‘Neukamerun’**).

blocks.title: Administration and economy
blocks.md: A governor represented the German emperor, with district officers and a colonial army. Germans used taxes and labour requirements. **Plantations** of cocoa, bananas, rubber and palm oil developed on fertile land, especially around Mount Cameroon. Railways and roads from Douala to the interior were begun to carry exports. Missions ran many schools, and German was taught in some.

blocks.caption: German Kamerun, 1884–1916.
blocks.alt: Timeline from 1880 to 1925 with 1884 treaty, 1911 Neukamerun, 1914 WWI begins and 1916 Germans leave.

blocks.title: African responses
blocks.md: Africans responded in different ways: some rulers cooperated, others resisted. Duala leaders protested against plans to move them from their land; their leader **Rudolf Duala Manga Bell** was executed in **August 1914** on a charge of treason. Resistance to German expansion also occurred inland and in the grassfields. Plantation labour and taxation were widely resented.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Neukamerun came in 1911, not in 1884.
- German rule lasted about 30 years, ending during the First World War.
- Do not describe African societies as passive: they used negotiation, resistance and adaptation.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Length of rule
blocks.statement: German rule began in 1884 and the Germans left in 1916. How long did it last?

blocks.title: Example 2 — Why plantations?
blocks.statement: Explain why plantations developed around Mount Cameroon.
steps: Volcanic soils are fertile and rainfall is high.
The coast made export to Europe easy.
Colonial authorities gave companies land and labour.
blocks.answer: Soil, climate and access to export, plus colonial policy.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Assess the view that economic motives were the main cause of the Scramble for Africa.
exercises.model: Economic motives were important: Europe needed raw materials, markets and secure investment. But political rivalry and national prestige, strategic routes, humanitarian and missionary arguments and new technology were also causes. In many cases political competition decided where and when claims were made. Economic motives were a main cause but not the only one.
